newsitem.title: USA: Ukraine cenbank gov sees IMF loan decision in Dec.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine cenbank gov sees IMF loan decision in Dec.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund should decide in December whether to grant Ukraine a new Extended Fund Facility loan of up to $3.0 billion, Ukrainian central bank governor Viktor Yushchenko said on Wednesday.
The former Soviet republic will then press on with negotiations with the Fund on a stabilisation loan for its new hryvnia currency, Yushchenko told Reuters in an interview.
He also said Ukraine planned to issue dollar-denominated short-term paper, ideally between nine months and one year in maturity.

Deputy Prime Minister for the economy Viktor Pynzenyk had said on Tuesday that details of the loan should be fixed when an IMF mission visits Kiev later this month. Ukraine has been in talks on a three-year EFF of $2.5 billion to 3.0 billion.
"The board of directors of the IMF is ready to decide this question in December 1996," Yushchenko said, adding the first tranche could be paid in the first quarter of 1997.
Conclusion of the EFF programme would be a condition for formal talks on the currency stabilisation fund, he said.
Ukraine introduced its hryvnia currency on September 2 and it has remained stable at 1.76 to the dollar.
Yushchenko said the stabilisation credit, up to a maximum $1.45 billion, would be an important political demonstration of support for Ukraine's currency reform.
"It is politically necessary but the talks themselves on the stabilisation fund are going on as a secondary question to the EFF," Yushchenko said.
He said the most important support for the hryvnia would be a sound economic policy.
"If the economy itself has no serious imbalances, no questions will arise about where money should come from to support the exchange rate," he said.
Ukraine is receiving an $876 million IMF standby credit.
Ukrainian officials have said the country plans to issue short-term securities in foreign currency.
Yushchenko said they would be in dollars. Asked about the maturity, he said, "Nine months to a year would be optimum."

He said details of the loan could only be discussed once the 1997 budget was adopted. The bank has said it will not issue inflationary credits to cover the deficit, of 3.8 percent of GDP (2.4 percent by Western calculations).
Yushchenko said the Ukraine team had discussed with the World Bank a credit of up $300 million to help restructure the financial system.
